strengths: Addresses a pivotal bottleneck in the practical adoption of diffusion-based LLMs: the lack of KV caching due to bidirectional attention and generation quality collapse during parallel token decoding.
Proposes a clean, training-free framework combining block-wise approximate KV caching (PrefixCache and DualCache) with confidence-aware dynamic parallel decoding.

Provides solid theoretical justification (Theorem 1) establishing conditions and bounds under which parallel decoding over independent marginals coincides with true joint greedy decoding in the high-confidence regime.

Extensive empirical evaluations across multiple models (LLaDA-Instruct, Dream-Base) and benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP) show substantial speedups (up to 27.6x in long-context settings) with negligible performance degradation.
weaknesses: Confidence-based thresholding has been previously explored in non-autoregressive text generation and iterative masked image/text generation (e.g., MaskGIT, Levenshtein Transformer); discussing and contrasting with this literature would better position the parallel decoding novelty.

The theoretical framework in Theorem 1 relies on the existence of a coherent, well-defined joint probability mass function from which marginals are derived, whereas discrete diffusion models typically predict position-wise marginals directly.

All benchmarks are evaluated with a batch size of 1 on a single GPU. Analysis on batched inference throughput and the memory overhead introduced by caching both prefix and suffix activations (DualCache) is omitted.

strengths: Addresses a timely and critical bottleneck in diffusion-based language models (Diffusion LLMs), namely the lack of KV caching and the severe latency associated with step-by-step or fixed-rate parallel decoding.

Proposes two pragmatic, training-free techniques: a block-wise approximate KV cache (PrefixCache and DualCache) leveraging temporal activation stability, and a confidence-thresholded parallel decoding rule.

Provides solid theoretical grounding in Theorem 1, establishing tight bounds under which greedy parallel decoding under the product of marginals is equivalent to decoding under the true joint distribution, alongside total variation and KL divergence bounds.

Demonstrates substantial, practical end-to-end speedups (ranging from 5x to over 27x depending on sequence length and prefill) across multiple standardized benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP) and two architectures (LLaDA and Dream) with negligible loss in downstream accuracy.
Includes helpful empirical analyses and ablations detailing the trade-offs of block size, confidence threshold, and activation cosine similarities across denoising steps.
weaknesses: Adopting block-wise generation fundamentally imposes an autoregressive block constraint on the diffusion generation process, which limits global bidirectional revision across different blocks—one of the core conceptual advantages of masked diffusion over autoregressive generation.

As acknowledged in Remark 1, the theoretical analysis relies on the assumption of a well-defined, coherent underlying joint probability mass function from which marginals are derived; masked diffusion models parameterized per-token do not strictly guarantee such joint consistency.

The evaluation compares exclusively against unoptimized vanilla diffusion model implementations (LLaDA, Dream); comparing throughput against competitive autoregressive baselines running on standard high-throughput inference engines (e.g., vLLM) or speculative decoding frameworks would provide clearer practical positioning.
There are minor presentation and typographical issues that should be cleaned up (e.g., 'hgiher' on page 2, duplicated 'takes takes' in Table 7).

strengths: High practical significance: Inference latency is currently the primary bottleneck hindering the deployment of discrete diffusion LLMs (such as LLaDA and Dream). Fast-dLLM provides an effective, training-free acceleration framework that directly addresses this limitation.

Complementary and well-motivated techniques: The combination of block-wise approximate KV caching (both PrefixCache and DualCache) for bidirectional attention and confidence-aware parallel unmasking is intuitive, well-engineered, and demonstrably synergistic.

Rigorous theoretical analysis: Theorem 1 provides formal guarantees showing that under high confidence ($p_j > 1 - \epsilon$ with $(n+1)\epsilon \le 1$), greedy parallel decoding is provably equivalent to greedy joint decoding, along with tight $L_p$ and KL divergence bounds.

Strong empirical results: The method achieves substantial throughput gains (up to 27.6× on long generation/prefill settings and 5×–11× in standard settings) across multiple tasks (GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP) and models (LLaDA and Dream) with minimal to no drop in accuracy.

Insightful ablations and analysis: The paper includes empirical validation of the underlying caching assumption (via activation cosine similarity heatmaps across diffusion steps), hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (cache block size, threshold $\tau$), and comparisons against fixed token-per-step baselines.
weaknesses: Compromising purely non-autoregressive bidirectional modeling: By enforcing a block-by-block left-to-right generation schedule, the model partially reverts to a semi-autoregressive paradigm, sacrificing the ability to iteratively refine arbitrary token spans globally across the entire sequence.

Evaluation restricted to structured reasoning and coding tasks: The benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP) primarily evaluate deterministic and low-entropy generation. It remains unclear how well the confidence thresholding mechanism and approximate cache generalize to open-ended, creative generation (e.g., MT-Bench or Chatbot Arena benchmarks) where model confidence is naturally lower and less calibrated.

Limited exploration of temperature and sampling dynamics: The theoretical formulation assumes greedy decoding. A discussion or experimental evaluation of how stochastic sampling (temperature > 0) interacts with confidence thresholding and parallel unmasking would provide a more complete picture.
Minor presentation issues: There are several minor typographical errors (e.g., page 2: 'achieves hgiher acceleration'; page 10: 'diffusion langauge models').

strengths: Addresses a crucial and timely bottleneck: the inference inefficiency of discrete/masked diffusion LLMs caused by full bidirectional attention (precluding standard KV caching) and quality degradation under naive parallel unmasking.
Proposes a simple, practical, and training-free solution combining block-wise approximate KV caching (including DualCache for prefix and suffix states) with confidence-aware parallel decoding.

Provides solid theoretical motivation (Theorem 1) establishing conditions under which greedy parallel decoding matches joint greedy decoding, which directly motivates the factor-based decoding algorithm.

Empirical evaluation is extensive and convincing, covering multiple diffusion LLMs (LLaDA, LLaDA-1.5, Dream, LLaDA-V multimodal) across four standard reasoning and code benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP) and multimodal benchmarks (MathVista, MathVerse).
Delivers substantial real-world speedups (up to 27.6x under longer sequence lengths) while consistently maintaining or even slightly improving generation accuracy across benchmarks.
weaknesses: The block-wise formulation essentially imposes an autoregressive ordering across blocks (left-to-right block generation), which restricts the arbitrary-order bidirectional generation capability inherent to full diffusion models.

The theoretical guarantees in Theorem 1 rely on the existence of a well-defined, consistent underlying joint PMF matching the marginals, an assumption that masked diffusion models do not strictly satisfy in practice (as acknowledged in Remark 1).

Throughput gains plateau at larger batch sizes (as shown in Figure 9) due to the compute-bound nature of iterative diffusion denoising compared to memory-bound autoregressive decoding, presenting a continuing challenge for high-concurrency serving.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely bottleneck: open-source Masked Diffusion LLMs (e.g., LLaDA, Dream) suffer from severe inference latency due to bidirectional attention precluding exact KV caching and quality degradation during aggressive parallel unmasking.

Proposes a practical, training-free approach combining block-wise approximate KV caching (PrefixCache and DualCache) with confidence-guided parallel decoding, requiring no retraining or architectural modifications.

Provides a sound theoretical justification (Theorem 1) establishing tight conditions under which greedy parallel decoding using independent marginals coincides with joint greedy decoding, directly motivating the adaptive factor-based decoding algorithm.

Thorough empirical evaluation across several models (LLaDA, LLaDA-1.5, Dream, LLaDA-V) and diverse benchmark suites (GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP, MathVista, MathVerse), demonstrating significant speedups (up to 27.6x) with minimal loss in task performance.
weaknesses: The block-wise generation scheme effectively turns the fully non-autoregressive diffusion model into a semi-autoregressive / block-autoregressive generator, partially sacrificing the theoretical global bidirectional revision capability inherent to diffusion models.

Approximation sensitivity varies across model types and tasks; for instance, the multimodal model LLaDA-V suffers significant accuracy drops (>8%) when using small block sizes, requiring an ad-hoc full-block refresh heuristic rather than the standard block cache mechanism.

The paper lacks comprehensive evaluation on long-range text generation or open-ended creative writing tasks, where global bidirectional coherence and multi-token consistency might be more vulnerable to caching approximations than in standard short-to-medium reasoning benchmarks.

As noted in the batch size analysis (Appendix C.5), diffusion LLMs remain compute-bound; the throughput advantages over optimized autoregressive baselines (e.g., LLaMA) deteriorate substantially at higher batch sizes.
Minor presentation flaws and typos exist in the draft (e.g., 'hgier acceleration' in the introduction contributions, and double periods in Figure 1 caption).

strengths: Addresses two critical and well-known bottlenecks in discrete diffusion LLMs (lack of KV caching due to bidirectional attention, and quality degradation under parallel decoding) without requiring any retraining.

Provides a solid theoretical grounding (Theorem 1) establishing the exact conditions under which greedy parallel decoding matches sequential greedy decoding, which directly motivates the factor-based decoding rule.

Achieves impressive end-to-end speedups (ranging from 5.3x to 27.6x depending on sequence length and shot setup) across multiple demanding reasoning and coding benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP) with minimal loss in task accuracy.
Demonstrates strong generality across diverse model families (LLaDA, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-7B) and modalities (vision-language reasoning via LLaDA-V on MathVista and MathVerse).
Presents thorough ablations and analyses, including cosine similarity heatmaps justifying KV cache reuse, block size trade-offs, and batch size scalability.
weaknesses: Adopting block-wise left-to-right generation partially re-introduces autoregressive ordering into diffusion LLMs, limiting the bidirectional context refinement across future blocks until subsequent blocks are decoded.

Multimodal models exhibit high sensitivity to block sizes (e.g., LLaDA-V accuracy drops by >8% on small block sizes in Table 9), requiring an alternative refresh-based heuristic rather than the standard block-wise cache.
The memory overhead of caching both prefix and suffix activations in DualCache is not thoroughly quantified in terms of peak GPU VRAM usage.

The paper would benefit from a broader discussion and empirical comparison against external acceleration baselines (e.g., speculative decoding or semi-autoregressive block models) beyond internal ablations against vanilla diffusion baselines.
